import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1106

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1064](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106)
-/

open Nat Finset Filter Topology

namespace Erdos1106

/-- The partition function p(n) is the number of ways to write n as a sum of positive
integers (where the order of the summands does not matter). -/
def p : ℕ → ℕ := fun n => Fintype.card (Nat.Partition n)

/--
Let $p(n)$ be the partition number of $n$ and $F(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of
$∏_{i= 1} ^ {n} p(n)$, then $F(n)$ tends to infinity when $n$ tends to infinity.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1106.parts.i :
    answer(sorry) ↔ Tendsto (fun n => #(∏ i ∈ Icc 1 n, p i).primeFactors) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

/--
Let $p(n)$ be the partition number of $n$ and $F(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of
$∏_{i= 1} ^ {n} p(n)$, $F(n)>n$ for sufficiently large $n$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1106.parts.ii :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᶠ n in atTop, #(∏ i ∈ Icc 1 n, p i).primeFactors > n := by
  sorry

end Erdos1106

findings.description: The docstring at line 34 writes ∏_{i=1}^n p(n), with a constant factor, rather than ∏_{i=1}^n p(i). This describes the prime divisors of p(n)^n, not those of the accumulated partition numbers. The Lean statement itself is correctly indexed. At n = 7, the documented product has 2 distinct prime factors, whereas the Lean product has 5; both counts were checked in Lean.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106 defines F(n) as the number of distinct prime factors of ∏_{1≤k≤n} p(k), and asks whether F(n) tends to infinity.
findings.suggested_fix: Change p(n) to p(i) inside the docstring's product. Leave the Lean right-hand side unchanged.

findings.description: The docstring at line 43 repeats the misindexed product ∏_{i=1}^n p(n), which equals p(n)^n. The Lean statement correctly uses ∏ i ∈ Icc 1 n, p i. Thus the documentation defines a different F from both the source and the formal statement.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106 uses the distinct prime factors of ∏_{1≤k≤n} p(k) and asks: “Is F(n)>n for all sufficiently large n?”
findings.suggested_fix: Change the product in the docstring to ∏_{i=1}^n p(i). Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

findings.description: The module reference at line 21 displays “erdosproblems.com/1064”, although its actual URL correctly points to problem 1106. This is a reference-label slip, not a defect in the formal mathematics.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106 identifies this partition-function problem as #1106.

status_issues.source_status: The divergence question has an affirmative solution. The source credits Schinzel's observation using the partition asymptotic and Tijdeman's result, with details in Erdős–Ivić (1990), p. 69. It also records the stronger bound F(n) ≫ log n proved by Schinzel and Wirsing (1987).
status_issues.evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106 explicitly says that Schinzel noted “F(n)→∞ follows from the asymptotic formula for p(n) and a result of Tijdeman” and that “Schinzel and Wirsing [ScWi87] have proved F(n) ≫ log n.” The page's overall OPEN label does not make this first, settled subquestion open.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change part (i) to category research solved and replace answer(sorry) with answer(True), retaining its right-hand side. Part (ii) should remain research open.

review.notes: All three declarations were checked. There are no misformalized Lean mathematical claims: p counts ordinary unordered integer partitions, and both theorem right-hand sides match the source exactly. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles without errors or warnings. It checks p(0),…,p(10), proves p(n)>0 and nonvanishing of every accumulated product, verifies the filter quantifier expansions, and proves monotonicity of the prime-divisor count. In particular, primeFactors' special zero value is unreachable, and the n=0 and n=1 boundary cases do not affect either asymptotic question.
